# Introducing Render Sandboxes: A computer for every agent

November 04, 2026

· Yaroslav Borets, Ammar Aijazi, and Azzam Aijazi

Today we’re launching Render Sandboxes in public beta. Render Sandboxes let you safely give your agents a computer to work with: a fully isolated Linux environment where they can install dependencies, edit files, and run code.

Each sandbox starts quickly, runs indefinitely, and automatically suspends when idle. You can reliably run thousands at once and lock down what each one can reach. You’re billed for CPU only when your agents are actually using it.

results.title: Render Sandboxes Computer for Every AI Agent: Public Beta Review
results.content:
Every Render sandbox is its own Firecracker microVM: a fully isolated Linux computer with its own filesystem, its own processes, and persistent state. That isolation is the whole point. An AI agent that installs packages, edits files, and runs code needs a machine of its own — not a corner of your application server, and not a shared container where one bad command can touch another user’s data. [...] ## What It Does in Practice

### 1. Run your agent inside a sandbox

Give your agents tools, files, and processes that persist between sessions. The canonical example is running an agent harness such as Claude Code or Codex inside the sandbox, so the agent has a real machine to work on rather than a stateless function call. Your product creates a sandbox through the SDK, uploads the task, streams the agent’s commands and output, and terminates the sandbox when the work is done. Because state persists across suspend and resume, a long-running task can pause for hours — waiting on a human approval, for instance — and continue without losing its place.

### 2. Spin up a full copy of your app [...] Snapshots are the other half of the story. A snapshot captures the filesystem, memory, and running processes of a sandbox, so a restored sandbox picks up exactly where it left off. You can also start new sandboxes from custom images or saved snapshots, so every agent begins from a prepared environment — dependencies installed, tools configured — instead of rebuilding the world on every run. Sandboxes started from the same image each get their own copy of the filesystem, so agents can run tests or work on different inputs in parallel without interfering with each other.
